tldr: By controlling exploration rewards toward contact candidates from a grasping algorithm using a dedicated critic head and a weight decay schedule, this paper shows that a quadrupedal mobile manipulator can learn and deploy non-prehensile transport (pushing/pulling) of complex furniture with high success rates.
hero_caption: Overview of this study. Using candidate interaction points from a general-purpose grasping algorithm as exploration guides, reinforcement learning enables a quadrupedal mobile manipulator to acquire skills for transporting complex objects such as chairs and tables to goal positions through contact.
overview:
Mobile manipulators that attach a robotic arm to a quadrupedal robot (locomanipulators) are well suited for moving heavy loads or bulky furniture in human environments. However, non-prehensile manipulation—such as pushing, pulling, or sliding large chairs that cannot be grasped directly with a gripper—is extremely difficult to control because it involves hybrid dynamics where system dynamics switch discontinuously depending on whether contact is made or broken. Traditional methods like Model Predictive Control (MPC) struggle with real-time replanning, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) suffers from contact sparsity where rewards cannot be obtained without finding contact. Consequently, robots often fall into local minima where they completely avoid contact to escape energy consumption penalties.

To solve this, the authors propose an approach that repurposes a general-purpose grasping candidate detection algorithm to sample candidate interaction points from object meshes and provides a dense exploration reward guiding the end-effector toward them. Crucially, rather than summing this exploration reward into a single scalar reward, they formulate the problem within a Multi-Critic RL framework with an independent exploration critic. The weight of the exploration critic is high early in training so the robot quickly learns how to establish contact, and it is linearly decayed (faded out) as training progresses. This recovers a task-optimal whole-body control policy freed from constraints toward specific contact points.

In simulation tasks such as chair transportation and box pushing, the proposed approach achieved a 94.1% task success rate, significantly outperforming conventional single-critic methods (PPO) and fixed-weight multi-critic baselines. Furthermore, the learned policy was deployed zero-shot onto the real quadrupedal mobile manipulator "ALMA", successfully transporting unseen chairs and a three-legged table, recovering autonomously from external disturbances, and transporting 6.5 kg furniture that exceeds the arm's rated payload capacity.
contributions: Proposal of a contact-guided exploration framework that generates candidate interaction points from a general-purpose grasping algorithm to efficiently encourage contact even on complex, non-convex objects

Implementation of a Multi-Critic PPO formulation that evaluates exploration, task, and regularization rewards with independent critic heads and gradually decays the exploration weight to transition toward a task-optimal policy
Systematic simulation evaluation across chair transportation, box pushing, and dishwasher opening tasks, achieving high task success rates
Demonstration on a physical quadrupedal mobile manipulator (ALMA) transporting unseen furniture, recovering from disturbances, and carrying payloads exceeding the arm's rated capacity

sections.heading: The Challenge of Non-Prehensile Manipulation and Contact-Guided Multi-Critic Learning
sections.summary: Non-prehensile manipulation to move bulky objects exceeding gripper payloads is promising, but contact discontinuities and difficult exploration have long posed challenges. This paper breaks through this exploration bottleneck by combining contact guidance from grasping candidate points with a weight decay schedule in Multi-Critic RL.
sections.details:
In unstructured environments like homes and warehouses, mobile manipulators must be able to reposition heavy or bulky objects freely. However, conventional pick-and-place approaches are severely restricted by gripper size and arm payload limits. Non-prehensile manipulation—such as pushing, pulling, and sliding—offers a powerful alternative.

Yet controlling non-prehensile manipulation is far from straightforward. Unlike grasping, the robot and object are not rigidly coupled, making the process dependent on discontinuous contact mechanics (hybrid dynamics) governed by unilateral contact constraints and friction cones. In mobile manipulation, floating-base stability, arm joint limits, and object motion must all be coordinated simultaneously. Model-based approaches like MPC often simplify physical models to reduce computational overhead, which limits real-time replanning when contacts slip or detach.

On the other hand, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) can learn contact-rich skills directly through trial and error. However, for extended whole-body coordination tasks, contact sparsity is a severe issue. Because positive rewards cannot be earned without accidentally exerting force in the correct direction, regularization penalties punishing unnatural motion or power consumption dominate. As a result, the robot often settles into a local minimum where it completely avoids touching the object to avoid penalties.

For simple shapes like boxes, sampling the surface uniformly can guide contact. But for non-convex objects with thin parts like chairs, most uniform samples are physically unviable contact points. To address this, the authors extract candidate interaction points using a general-purpose grasping algorithm and design a dense exploration reward guiding the end-effector toward them. In addition, they assign a dedicated critic to this exploration reward and gradually decay its influence as training proceeds, enabling a smooth transition from early contact discovery to late-stage task optimization.

sections.heading: Limitations of Prior Approaches and the Paper's Positioning
sections.summary: Prior works in non-prehensile manipulation and locomanipulation often depended on exact physical modeling or human demonstrations. This study learns policies from scratch without demonstrations, relying instead on object-centric contact priors and multi-critic reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
Reviewing prior works highlights the unique strengths of the proposed approach.

- Non-Prehensile Manipulation Lineage:
Historically, pushing and sliding operations on known convex objects were studied using analytical mechanics of contact modes. Recently, MPC has been applied to mobile manipulators, but it requires accurate 3D mesh models, and online replanning upon contact slip or loss is computationally demanding.

- RL-Based Locomanipulation:
Successful examples of locomanipulation using RL, such as opening doors or pushing obstacles, are increasing. However, because reaching solutions via random exploration is difficult, many studies rely on motion capture demonstrations, teleoperation, or visual pre-training. Collecting high-quality demonstrations for dynamic non-prehensile manipulation is costly and lacks scalability. In contrast, this study uses no demonstration data, learning policies from scratch guided by contact priors derived from object geometry.

- Multi-Critic and Curriculum Learning:
Mixing opposing objectives—approaching and establishing contact with an object (exploration) versus transporting it stably to a goal (task completion)—into a single scalar reward causes gradient interference and local minima. Multi-critic methods train independent value functions (critics) for each reward component, enabling stable gradient estimation and dynamic adjustment of objective ratios. This study leverages this structure by introducing a weight decay curriculum that gradually reduces the contribution of the exploration critic.

sections.heading: Sampling Contact Candidates and the Multi-Critic Architecture
sections.summary: A grasping algorithm extracts 25 candidate interaction points from furniture meshes to provide an end-effector reaching exploration reward. By evaluating exploration, task, and regularization rewards across three independent critic heads and decaying the exploration weight, the system safely transitions from contact seeking to whole-body task optimization.
sections.details:
The proposed system has a hierarchical structure where a high-level policy outputs whole-body commands and a low-level locomotion controller tracks them.

The high-level policy actions are target arm joint angles $q^{*}_{a}$ (6 DoF), target base planar velocities $(v^{*}_{x}, v^{*}_{y}, \omega^{*}_{z})$, and target base height $h^{*}$. Actively modulating base height is crucial: extending the arm low and forward to touch near the floor pushes the shoulder joint to its limit, triggering safety stops. Lowering the base avoids arm singularities and joint limits. The low-level controller incorporates a pre-trained locomotion policy that tracks base velocity and height commands.

- Exploration and Contact Candidate Sampling (Section 3.1):
A general-purpose grasping algorithm is applied to the object CAD mesh to extract 25 candidate interaction points (Fig. F3). At the start of an episode, one target point $\mathbf{p}_{target}$ is chosen, and a dense exploration reward $r_{\text{exp}}$ guides the end-effector toward it. Too few points cause the policy to overfit to that specific location, hindering task completion, while too many points resemble uniform sampling and reduce exploration efficiency; 25 points struck the optimal balance. For the simple box-pushing task, conventional uniform surface sampling was used.

- Multi-Critic Formulation (Section 3.2):
Rewards are decomposed into three groups: task performance $r_{\text{task}}$, exploration incentive $r_{\text{exp}}$, and motion regularization $r_{\text{reg}}$. PPO is extended with dedicated critic heads for each group. The composite advantage used for policy updates is computed as $A_{t} = \sum_{h=1}^{3} w_{h} A_{t}^{h}$. This allows flexible control over the exploration weight $w_{\text{exp}}$ during training.

- Training Details and Weight Schedule (Section 3.3):
Training was conducted in Isaac Lab across 4,096 parallel environments. Chair models included 15 IKEA models alongside 100 procedurally generated models with randomized dimensions. In the multi-critic weight schedule, the task weight is kept fixed at $w_{\text{task}} = 0.75$, while the exploration weight $w_{\text{exp}}$ decays linearly from $0.1$ to $0.01$ between 5,000 and 10,000 steps. Concurrently, the regularization weight $w_{\text{reg}}$ increases from $0.15$ to $0.24$. Fading out the exploration reward once contacts can be reliably established allows the policy to converge on task efficiency and stability.

sections.heading: 94.1% Simulation Success Rate and Robust Real-World Deployment
sections.summary: The proposed approach achieved a 94.1% success rate in simulated chair transportation, significantly outperforming single-critic and fixed-weight baselines. Real-world experiments demonstrated transport of unseen furniture (69.0% success rate), autonomous recovery from disturbances, transport of 6.5 kg loads exceeding the arm's rated capacity, and a two-stage dishwasher opening sequence.
sections.details:
Experiments thoroughly evaluated the proposed method (Multi-Critic PPO + WS) against baselines and through real-world deployment.

- Quantitative Evaluation and Ablations (Section 4.1):
The method was compared with standard PPO (single critic), PPO+WS with scheduled scalar reward weights, and Multi-Critic PPO with fixed weights. Standard PPO had a high Missed Contact rate of 9.1% due to failing to discover contacts, and removing the exploration reward entirely resulted in a 0% success rate. With fixed-weight Multi-Critic, contact was established, but persistent adherence to contact points increased the Tipover rate. In contrast, the proposed method achieved a 94.1% success rate with only a 4.4% tipover rate, showing high stability across seeds with a standard deviation of 0.98%.

- Emergent Behaviors (Section 4.2):
Visualizing the learned policy revealed that it intelligently chooses which side of the chair to approach based on the goal position (Fig. F4). Coordinated whole-body motions naturally emerged: selecting contact locations that maximize control authority along the travel direction and having the base track properly to prevent arm joint limit violations.

- Real-World Deployment and Zero-Shot Generalization (Section 4.3):
The learned policy was deployed zero-shot (without real-world fine-tuning) onto the ALMA quadrupedal robot. When evaluated across four unseen IKEA furniture items (ADDE, SANDSBERG, folding chair VIHALS, and 3-legged table LOVBACKEN), it achieved an overall success rate of 69.0% (40/58 trials) (Fig. F6). Even on the backrest-free 3-legged table, the robot adapted by hooking its arm around the legs. Furthermore, it demonstrated recovery behaviors by widening arm swings to re-hook contacts when lost (Fig. F7), robustness to sudden human perturbations pulling the chair (Fig. F8 (b)), and transportation of a 6.5 kg payload exceeding the arm's rated capacity (Fig. F8 (a)).

- Articulated Object Manipulation (Section 4.4):
In the dishwasher opening task, contact sequencing naturally emerged: the robot first pulled the handle to crack the door open, then switched contact to push the top panel down until fully horizontal (Fig. F9). Standard PPO tended to pull forcefully on the handle and stick near joint limits, whereas the proposed method reduced time spent near joint limits (within 10%) by 59%.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: Combining Multi-Critic RL with contact-guided exploration establishes an efficient, robust framework for complex non-prehensile locomanipulation. Moving away from external motion capture systems and adopting adaptive curriculum tuning remain key future challenges.
sections.details:
This study offers a clear solution to the long-standing problem of local minima in non-prehensile manipulation by separating and dynamically decaying an exploration critic. Demonstrating on hardware that whole-body contact dynamics and quadrupedal locomotion can cooperate to move heavy objects well beyond the arm's nominal payload—by leveraging ground support forces—is a significant milestone.

However, limitations remain. First, physical experiments rely on an external motion capture system for object pose estimation, preventing immediate deployment in outdoor or arbitrary real-world environments. Second, the critic weight decay schedule is manually tuned as a hyperparameter; introducing an adaptive curriculum that adjusts weights automatically based on learning progress is a promising direction for future work.

takeaways: In non-prehensile manipulation of bulky objects that cannot be grasped, whole-body coordination leveraging floating-base mobility and ground reaction forces provides essential strength beyond arm capacity alone.

Dense exploration rewards interfere with task completion if added directly into a scalar reward; separating them into a multi-critic framework and decaying their weight over training is highly effective.
Grasping algorithms can be directly repurposed beyond grasping as geometric prior extractors to identify where to establish contact in non-prehensile manipulation.
Actively lowering the quadrupedal robot base height (lowered by ~15 cm in this work) dramatically prevents arm singularities and shoulder joint limit violations.
limitations: Relies on an external motion capture (MoCap) system for object tracking in real-world environments, falling short of autonomous operation using only onboard cameras.
The exploration critic weight decay timing (5k to 10k steps) follows a fixed linear schedule, requiring manual tuning across tasks and environments.
Odometry error accumulation during rapid yaw turns in real-world runs caused occasional failures where the robot tipped furniture over during lateral approaches.
